title: Bigsky widow sues
subtitle: Woman seeks damages, citing 'needless killing'
article: Rose Ann Bigsky, 32, is also suing the Attorney General of Canada for the way the RCMP treated her after the shooting on Highway 41, which occurred during a violent confrontation between her husband, Melvin Bigsky, and an RCMP officer.

Bigsky claims in court documents that the RCMP arrested her without cause and held her in a jail cell, splattered with her husband's blood, until the next afternoon. She was not allowed to speak with a lawyer, was never read her rights and was not told until the next day that her husband had died at the scene of the shooting.

She is asking for punitive and general damages and financial compensation for the loss of Melvin Bigsky as the provider for her and her children, who are nine, six and two years old. The children are Rose Ann's from a previous relationship, but Bigsky was financially responsible for them, the claim states.
The claim does not specify an amount for damages.
Justice Department officials have not yet been served with the court documents, said RCMP spokesperson Heather Russell.
RCMP are still investigating the incident that happened about 8:30 p.m. on April 27.

If there are no criminal charges laid as a result of the investigation then, as usually occurs in cases of police shootings, a coroner's inquest is called to draw out the facts, said Saskatchewan Justice Department spokesperson Jeff Bohach.
In her statement of claim Bigsky outlined the events of April 27 and 28.
She and her husband of one year, Melvin Bigsky, were passengers in a GMC Sierra truck driven by their friend, Ivan Indian. The trio was travelling south on Highway 41 toward Saskatoon from Nipawin.
According to her statement of claim, a police officer pulled them over, parked behind the truck and got out of the car. The officer placed Indian in the back seat of the cruiser.
Then an altercation occurred between the officer and Melvin Bigsky, during which Bigsky was sprayed in the face with pepper spray, the document states.
Melvin then got in behind the wheel of the truck, despite orders from the officer to get out because he was under arrest for impaired driving.
Rose Ann Bigsky states that she got out of the truck, protesting that Indian, not her husband, had been driving.
The officer told her to mind her own business or he would arrest her for obstructing a police officer.

Melvin then followed orders to get on his knees and placed his hands behind his back. The officer had placed handcuffs on one of his hands when Rose Ann asked again why her husband was being arrested. The officer told her he would arrest her too and pushed her away with his hands.
When Melvin saw that he told the officer to leave her alone.
The officer hit Melvin on the back with a baton and Melvin grabbed the officer. The two men fell to the ground and wrestled.
The pair broke apart, the officer ran to the cruiser and the Bigskys got into the truck with Melvin at the wheel.
"In an attempt to turn the truck around in order to leave the scene, the truck became hung up," the document states.
"The truck was disabled in that it could not proceed neither forward nor backwards."
The statement does not say anything about Melvin ramming the police car with the truck, as the police and Indian have said he did.
It goes on to say that Rose Ann told Melvin to give up and that he put his arms out of the driver's side window and shouted, "I give up."

"The police officer was approximately 50 feet away, had his revolver out and commenced walking towards the truck. Melvin Bigsky was again shouting, \`I give up,' then (Rose Ann) heard several gun shots.
"Melvin Bigsky turned to the Plaintiff and said \`That f---er is shooting at us.' Melvin Bigsky then fell over on top of the Plaintiff," the document states.
Rose Ann tried to get Melvin off her. Then she ran towards the police officer, asking him why he was shooting. The officer told her to get on the ground. Instead, she returned to Melvin in the truck.
She was with him, begging him not to leave her, when other officers arrived and told her to get away.
"Two police officers grabbed (her) and roughly placed her in the back seat of a City of Saskatoon police cruiser.
"The Plaintiff sat in the police cruiser for a long time at the scene, asking the police to pick up Melvin Bigsky, because (he) was hanging out of the truck door."
She was taken to the RCMP station in Saskatoon, searched and put in a cell without having her rights read to her, she states.
She was told she was being held as a material witness.
When she tried to phone her lawyer, she was unable to contact him and was denied further requests to try again.
Bigsky states that she "was left in the cell with bloody feet, clothing and with her husband's blood splattered all over her body. The Plaintiff asked to shower but was denied the right to do so."
A male and a female officer came to her cell the next morning and told her to take off her clothes. She was not allowed to shower but eventually changed her clothes as ordered.
Although she asked, no one would tell her if her husband was alive or dead, she states.
She was required to speak with a female officer before being released around 3 p.m. It was then she learned her husband had died. She was not offered grief counselling.

Bigsky claims the Attorney General of Canada is liable for the acts of the RCMP officers against her, including false arrest and false imprisonment, assault and battery, deprivation of liberty and visiting indignities upon her.
She also claims they are responsible for the wrongful death of Melvin Bigsky.

"The Plaintiff states that the manner in which she was confined and treated constitutes conduct by the defendant that is reprehensible, offensive or ordinary standards of morality and was a grave affront to human decency, a breach of trust of the police officer's oath of office," the claim states.
"The treatment of the Plaintiff resulted from RCMP policy and directives and as such constitute a systematic and deliberate violation of the Plaintiff," the document states.
Bigsky also claims the police violated her constitutional rights to life, liberty and security of the person as well as not to be subjected to cruel and unusual treatment or punishment.
Bigsky says she has recurring nightmares, sleeplessness, headaches, nervous shock and trauma, besides having lost her husband and her children's father.
